Eleanor Thorne believed that the soul of a community thrived only in the absence of locked doors. Her world was a web of shared obligations, where every private corner—closets of sentiment, drawers of solitude—must be opened to the collective gaze. She championed neighborhood councils that decided each family’s meals, co-ops that pooled wages, and open-floor apartments where silence was a form of hoarding. To Eleanor, privacy was the first betrayal, a seed of selfishness that grew into social rot. She cared most about dissolving the boundary between public and private, stitching every life into the common quilt until no thread was left unaccounted.

Her blind spot was as vast as her devotion. Eleanor could not see that by refusing to plant anything that grew in shade, she had starved the soil. She tore down fences without building windbreaks, emptied the pantry to feed tonight’s potluck while the winter storehouses went bare. Her decisions—always immediate, always for the visible good—sowed exhaustion. The old were left without rest, the young without secrets. She could not understand why enthusiasm waned, why people drifted away, why the gardens failed after the first flush. Tomorrow was a word that meant nothing to her; she lived in the relentless, crowded bright of now, never noticing that it was always, slowly, becoming night.

She never saved, only shared. The slow rot of a neglected foundation, the quiet erosion of a relationship starved of privacy, the long, slow poison of deferred maintenance—these were invisible to her. She was the perfect steward of the hour, and the unwitting architect of the ruin that would follow the dawn.

She knows whose dog barked at three in the morning, whose recycling bin is perpetually overflowing, and which teenager’s car arrives too late. She leaves casseroles for the grieving, posts neighborhood watch schedules by the mailboxes, and has a key to every house on the block. Privacy, to Margaret, is a kind of selfish silence—a door slammed in the face of collective care. She polices these boundaries with fierce love, shaming the new couple who fenced their backyard, whispering about the old man who keeps his blinds drawn. The community is her body, and she will not let it suffer a single cell of disconnection. But the future is a ghost she cannot see. Her attention is a furious present tense: the block party must happen *now*, the petition must be signed *today*. The roof she didn’t fix last summer now leaks into the crawlspace, and the soil under the community garden is poisoned by decades of neglect. She will not hear of the climate report or the school board’s budget cuts; those are distant bureaucracies. Her world is a beautifully tended house whose foundation is rotting. Margaret keeps the porch light burning, never noticing the night that is slowly, silently swallowing the whole street.

Her own life’s seams were unraveling, but she could not look away from her neighbors long enough to notice.
